idiom_name: no per-object lock exists; ownership by a worker plus message passing (Web Locks API across contexts)
implementation_notes: JavaScript runs one realm on one thread over one heap, so two scripts cannot touch the same object concurrently and the problem the pattern solves does not arise inside a realm. Concurrency returns at the edges: Web Workers and node:worker_threads run in separate realms and share memory only by transferring ArrayBuffer values or sharing SharedArrayBuffer (with Atomics for synchronisation), while browser tabs and workers coordinate through the Web Locks API, which publishes named, origin-scoped locks for a resource name rather than a lock attached to an object. The idiomatic replacement is therefore ownership: one worker owns the state and everyone else talks to it by message passing; use Atomics only for flat numeric shared buffers, which is a different, data-oriented design.
pitfalls: A blocking mutex cannot exist on the main thread: Atomics.wait is not allowed there, and a synchronous spin would freeze the page or the event loop instead of the caller.
SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers); without them there is no shared memory at all and every design must be message passing.

Web Locks are cooperative, per-origin and released when the callback settles: a lock held across an unawaited promise or a crashed tab stalls other tabs, and nothing prevents same-context code from ignoring the lock.
Worker state is not shared, so 'locking the object' is meaningless: copying data into a worker instead of transferring it silently duplicates state.
alternative: Keep the shared state inside one owner - a Web Worker or a node:worker_threads worker - and exchange messages; use the Web Locks API only for cross-tab/cross-context coordination by resource name.
